title: Life of a request
tagline: Every design starts by knowing exactly which hops a request takes and what each costs.
explain:
A request crosses many systems before you see a response. Knowing each hop lets you decide where to cache, where to scale and where latency hides.

1. DNS turns a name into an IP. Results are cached by TTL, so changing records is slow to propagate.
2. TCP and TLS add round trips before the first byte (a TLS 1.3 handshake is 1 RTT; reused connections skip it).
3. A CDN edge answers static and cacheable content close to the user, which removes the origin from the path entirely.
4. A load balancer (L4 or L7) terminates TLS and chooses a healthy backend.
5. The app server runs business logic. Authentication, validation and orchestration happen here.
6. A cache serves hot data in under a millisecond; on a miss the database is queried and the cache is filled.
7. The response travels back, often compressed.

Rule of thumb: every network hop in the same datacenter costs ~0.5 ms, cross-region 50-150 ms, and a disk read 0.1-10 ms. Most latency problems are too many sequential hops or one slow dependency, not slow code.
tradeoffs: More cache layers lower latency and load but add staleness and invalidation complexity.
A CDN is cheap and fast for cacheable data but cannot help personalized or write-heavy traffic.
Keeping connections warm saves RTTs but costs memory on servers and load balancers.
pitfalls: Forgetting DNS TTLs when planning failover.
Doing N sequential calls per request instead of one batched call (N+1).
Putting a CDN in front of responses that vary per user without the right cache key.
interview: Walk through what happens between pressing Enter and seeing the page.
Where would you add caching for a read-heavy product page and why?

title: Back-of-envelope estimation
tagline: Numbers decide the architecture. Estimate first, then choose components.
explain:
Estimation turns a vague product into engineering constraints. Do it in a fixed order and say every assumption aloud.

- Users: daily active users (DAU), then concurrent users (often 5-10% of DAU at peak).
- Traffic: requests per day / 86,400 = average QPS. Multiply by 2-5x for peak. Separate reads from writes.
- Storage: records per day x size x 365 x years x replication factor (usually 3).
- Bandwidth: QPS x payload size, ingress and egress separately.
- Compute: peak QPS / requests one server can handle, plus 30% headroom. For ML, divide tokens per second by tokens per GPU per second.
- Memory for caching: the hot working set (often 20% of data serves 80% of reads).

Useful anchors: 1M requests/day is ~12 QPS; a single Postgres primary handles roughly 5-20k simple QPS; Redis ~100k ops/s; one Kafka partition ~10-50 MB/s; a modern SSD 100k+ IOPS. Powers of ten are enough; accuracy within 2-3x is the goal.

Then interpret: if peak writes are 50k QPS you need sharding or a log-structured store; if the working set fits in 64 GB, one Redis node may do.
tradeoffs: Over-precise numbers waste time; being off by 10x changes the design, being off by 20% does not.
Planning for peak wastes money; planning for average falls over. Use autoscaling plus load shedding.
pitfalls: Mixing bits and bytes, or per-day and per-second.
Forgetting replication and indexes when sizing storage.
Ignoring write amplification and growth.
interview: Estimate storage and QPS for a service with 100M DAU posting twice a day.
How many GPUs to serve 3,000 LLM requests/s?

title: Networking essentials
tagline: The handful of protocol facts that come up in every design discussion.
explain:
You do not need to be a network engineer, but you must reason about these:

- Layers: L3 (IP routing), L4 (TCP/UDP, ports), L7 (HTTP, gRPC). Load balancers operate at L4 or L7.
- TCP gives ordered, reliable delivery with a handshake, congestion control and retransmission. Cost: connection setup, head-of-line blocking. UDP is connectionless and lossy; QUIC (HTTP/3) builds reliability on UDP and removes head-of-line blocking across streams.
- HTTP/1.1: one request at a time per connection. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one connection. HTTP/3 uses QUIC.
- TLS: encrypts and authenticates. mTLS authenticates both sides, common between services.
- Realtime options: short polling (simple, wasteful), long polling, Server-Sent Events (one-way stream over HTTP, ideal for LLM tokens), WebSockets (bidirectional, stateful, harder to scale), WebRTC (peer media, voice and video).
- DNS and GeoDNS steer traffic; anycast routes one IP to the nearest site.
- Timeouts: always set connect, read and overall deadlines, and propagate deadlines downstream.
tradeoffs: WebSockets give low latency both ways but need sticky connection management and reconnect logic; SSE is simpler for server push.
gRPC is efficient and typed but less browser-friendly than REST.
pitfalls: No timeouts: one slow dependency exhausts all threads.
Assuming the network is reliable or has bounded latency.
Load balancer idle timeouts killing long streams.
interview: SSE vs WebSockets for chat and for streaming LLM output?
Why can head-of-line blocking hurt HTTP/2 over TCP?

title: API design
tagline: Contracts that stay stable while everything behind them changes.
explain:
Good APIs make the system's behavior predictable for clients and operable for you.

- Resources and verbs: nouns in paths (/orders/42), HTTP methods for intent, correct status codes (201 created, 202 accepted for async work, 409 conflict, 429 with Retry-After).
- Idempotency: GET, PUT and DELETE should be safe to retry; make POST retry-safe with an Idempotency-Key header and store the first result.
- Pagination: use cursors (keyset), not offsets, for large or changing collections; return an opaque next_cursor.
- Errors: a consistent body with a stable machine code, human message and request id.
- Evolution: add optional fields only, never repurpose fields, version when you must break, and monitor who uses old versions.
- Long operations: return 202 with a job id and a status endpoint (or webhook / SSE) instead of holding the connection.
- Protocol choice: REST for public simplicity, gRPC for internal low-latency typed calls, GraphQL when clients need flexible shapes (beware N+1 and cost control).
- Security: authentication, authorization per resource, rate limits per key, input validation, no secrets in URLs.
tradeoffs: GraphQL reduces round trips but makes caching and cost control harder.
Strict versioning protects clients but multiplies maintenance.
pitfalls: Offset pagination on big tables.
Non-idempotent writes behind retrying clients (double charges).
Leaking internal IDs or schema details.
interview: Design the API for creating a payment safely.
How do you paginate a feed that gets new items constantly?

title: Data modeling
tagline: Start from access patterns, then pick the schema and the store.
explain:
Model data for the queries you must serve fast.

1. List entities and relationships (user, order, item) and the top 5 queries with their frequency.
2. Relational: normalize to avoid duplication, use foreign keys and transactions; add indexes for each query path. Works well to a few TB and thousands of QPS on one primary.
3. NoSQL (DynamoDB, Cassandra): model per access pattern, denormalize on purpose, choose a partition key that spreads load and groups what you read together, and a sort key for ordering and range scans.
4. Large or immutable blobs live in object storage; the database holds metadata and the key.
5. Time-ordered data (events, messages, metrics) is append-heavy: partition by time or entity and keep recent data hot.
6. Use stable unique ids and decide on soft deletes, auditing and tenant isolation (tenant_id on every row).

Signals to denormalize: a hot read needs joins across shards, or you read a derived value far more often than it changes. The cost is write complexity and risk of drift, so own an owner for each copy.
tradeoffs: Normalization saves space and keeps one source of truth, but joins cost at scale.
Denormalization makes reads fast but multiplies write paths.
pitfalls: Choosing a partition key by what is convenient, not by load distribution (hot partitions).
Storing blobs in the primary database.
Forgetting tenant isolation in the model.
interview: Design the schema for a chat app that must fetch latest messages per conversation.
When would you denormalize?

title: Database indexing
tagline: Indexes turn scans into lookups, and every index taxes your writes.
explain:
Without an index a query reads every row. An index is an extra sorted or hashed structure pointing to rows.

- B-tree (default in Postgres/MySQL): sorted, supports equality, range and ordering. Reads are O(log n); pages are updated in place, so random writes cost more.
- LSM tree (Cassandra, RocksDB, many NoSQL stores): writes go to memory and a log, then flush to immutable sorted files that are merged by compaction. Very fast writes, reads check several files (bloom filters help).
- Hash index: equality only.
- Composite index (a, b, c): helps queries filtering on a, a+b, a+b+c in that left-to-right order. Put equality columns first, then range columns.
- Covering index: contains all columns a query needs, avoiding a table lookup.
- Partial and expression indexes shrink and target indexes.
- Inverted index (search engines): term to document list. Spatial indexes (geohash, quadtree, R-tree) for location. Vector indexes (HNSW, IVF) for similarity.

Cost: each index slows inserts and updates and uses memory. Use EXPLAIN to verify a query uses the index you expect, and drop unused ones.
tradeoffs: More indexes make reads faster and writes slower and larger.
LSM favors write throughput; B-trees favor read latency and predictability.
pitfalls: Low-selectivity indexes (a boolean) that the planner ignores.
Wrong column order in composite indexes.
Functions on indexed columns that prevent index use.
interview: Why is a composite index (a,b) useless for a query filtering only on b?
B-tree vs LSM: when would you pick each?

title: Caching
tagline: The cheapest way to buy speed, and the easiest way to serve wrong data.
explain:
A cache keeps a copy of expensive-to-get data close to the consumer.

Where: browser, CDN edge, API gateway, application memory, a distributed cache (Redis, Memcached), database buffer pool.

Patterns:

- Cache-aside: app checks cache, on miss reads the DB and fills the cache. Most common; the app owns consistency.
- Read-through / write-through: the cache layer loads or writes to the store for you. Simpler for callers, consistent writes, slower writes.
- Write-back: write to cache and flush later. Fast but risks data loss on failure.

Invalidation: TTLs (simple, bounded staleness), explicit delete on write, versioned keys, or event-driven invalidation from change streams.

Problems and fixes:

- Stampede (hot key expires, thousands of misses): single-flight/request coalescing, jittered TTLs, refresh-ahead, serve-stale-while-revalidate.
- Penetration (requests for keys that do not exist): cache negative results or use a Bloom filter.
- Hot keys: replicate across nodes or add a small local cache.
- Eviction: LRU is the default; LFU for stable popularity.

A hit rate of 90% vs 99% means 10x less load on the database. The database must still survive a cold or failed cache.
tradeoffs: Higher TTLs cut load but serve staler data.
Write-through keeps consistency but doubles write latency; write-back is fastest but can lose writes.
pitfalls: Caching without a plan for invalidation.
Cache as source of truth.
Cold-start thundering herd after a deploy or cache failure.
interview: Explain a cache stampede and three ways to prevent it.
How do you keep cache and database consistent on updates?

title: Sharding and consistent hashing
tagline: Split data across machines so adding a machine moves only a small slice.
explain:
Sharding (partitioning) splits a dataset across nodes when one machine cannot hold or serve it.

Choosing the shard key is the key decision. It must spread load evenly, keep common queries on one shard, and rarely change. Strategies: hash (even, but range scans scatter), range (good scans, hot-spot risk with sequential keys), directory (flexible lookup table).

Naive hash(key) mod N breaks when N changes: nearly every key maps to a different node, causing a massive reshuffle. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring; a key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding or removing a node moves only ~1/N of keys. Virtual nodes give each server many ring positions to even out load and allow weighted capacity.

Online resharding: use many small logical shards (for example 4,096) mapped to few physical nodes, and move logical shards between nodes while dual-writing or using change capture.

Costs of sharding: cross-shard joins and transactions, global uniqueness, rebalancing and hot keys (split the key, or isolate it). Try replicas and caching before sharding.
tradeoffs: Hash sharding balances load but loses range scans.
More virtual nodes means smoother balance but larger routing metadata.
pitfalls: Sharding by a low-cardinality or skewed key.
Using timestamp as a range shard key (all writes hit the newest shard).
Sharding too early.
interview: Explain consistent hashing and why virtual nodes matter.
How would you reshard a live 20 TB database?

title: Replication and lag
tagline: Copies buy availability and read throughput, and introduce time-travel bugs.
explain:
Replication keeps copies of data on multiple nodes.

- Single-leader: one primary takes writes and streams a log to followers. Simple, strong ordering; failover needs promotion and fencing.
- Multi-leader: multiple regions accept writes; conflicts must be resolved (last-write-wins, CRDTs, application logic).
- Leaderless (Dynamo style): writes go to several replicas; reads use quorums and repair stale copies.

Synchronous replication waits for followers (durable, slower, availability depends on followers). Asynchronous returns immediately (fast, but a failover can lose recent writes and followers lag).

Lag causes visible anomalies: a user writes then reads from a stale replica (violates read-your-writes); two reads go to different replicas and time appears to move backward (monotonic reads). Mitigations: read from the primary shortly after a write, route a session to one replica, or attach a version token and wait for the replica to catch up.

Failover hazards: split brain (two primaries) is prevented with quorum-based leader election and fencing tokens.
tradeoffs: Async replication maximizes speed and availability but risks data loss and staleness.
Reading from replicas scales reads but complicates correctness.
pitfalls: Assuming replicas are instantly up to date.
Failover without fencing the old primary.
Not measuring replication lag.
interview: How do you provide read-your-writes with async replicas?
What can go wrong during automatic failover?

title: CAP and PACELC
tagline: What a system must give up when the network breaks, and what it trades even when it works.
explain:
During a network partition a replicated system must pick: remain consistent (linearizable) by refusing some requests, or remain available by answering with possibly stale data. Partitions are a fact of networks, so 'pick two of three' is misleading: you choose C or A when a partition happens.

PACELC extends it: if Partitioned choose A or C; Else (normal operation) choose Latency or Consistency. Strong consistency across regions costs round trips, so even healthy systems trade latency for consistency.

Examples: etcd, ZooKeeper, Spanner favor consistency (minority side stops). Dynamo-style stores and Cassandra favor availability with tunable consistency.

Practical use: decide per feature. A bank balance and inventory counts usually need consistency; a like counter or feed does not. Many products mix: strongly consistent writes for money, eventual for the timeline.

Consistency is a spectrum: linearizable, sequential, causal, session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads), eventual. Choose the weakest that keeps the product correct.
tradeoffs: Strong consistency simplifies reasoning but reduces availability and adds latency.
Eventual consistency scales and stays available but pushes conflict handling into the app.
pitfalls: Calling a database 'CP' or 'AP' without specifying configuration.
Confusing CAP consistency with ACID consistency.
interview: Explain CAP without saying 'pick two'.
Which parts of an e-commerce system need strong consistency?

title: Quorums
tagline: Overlapping majorities are how replicas agree without a single point of failure.
explain:
With N replicas, a write must be acknowledged by W and a read must consult R replicas. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps the most recent write set in at least one replica, so the read can see the latest version (it picks the highest version number).

Common settings for N=3: W=2, R=2 (balanced, tolerates one node down); W=3, R=1 (fast reads, writes need every node); W=1, R=3 (fast writes). Dynamo-style systems expose these as tunable consistency levels (ONE, QUORUM, ALL).

Limits: quorums alone do not give linearizability. Concurrent writes, sloppy quorums with hinted handoff, clock-based last-write-wins and partial failures can still produce stale or lost updates. Systems add version vectors, read repair (fixing stale replicas during reads) and anti-entropy (background Merkle-tree comparison). Strong guarantees need consensus (Raft, Paxos).

Majority quorums are also the basis of consensus: any two majorities share a node, which is why Raft needs 3 nodes to tolerate 1 failure and 5 to tolerate 2.
tradeoffs: Higher W improves durability and read freshness at the cost of write latency and availability.
Higher R gives fresher reads at the cost of read latency.
pitfalls: Assuming R+W>N means linearizable.
Ignoring failed or slow nodes when counting acknowledgements.
interview: With N=5, what do W=3,R=3 tolerate? What about W=1,R=1?
How does read repair work?

title: Consensus: Raft
tagline: How a cluster elects a leader and agrees on an ordered log despite failures.
explain:
Consensus lets nodes agree on a sequence of commands even when some crash. Raft makes it understandable by separating leader election from log replication.

- Roles: follower, candidate, leader. Time is split into terms.
- Election: a follower that hears no heartbeat before a randomized timeout becomes a candidate, increments the term and requests votes. A node votes once per term and only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date. A majority wins. Randomized timeouts make split votes rare.
- Replication: the leader appends client commands to its log and sends AppendEntries to followers. An entry is committed once stored on a majority, then applied to the state machine.
- Safety: a new leader always has every committed entry, because any two majorities overlap.
- Reads: serve through the leader after confirming leadership (ReadIndex) or with leases, otherwise a deposed leader can return stale data.

Use: etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV and most control planes (Kubernetes stores its state in etcd). Do not put high-volume data through consensus; use it for metadata, locks and leader election.

With 5 nodes you tolerate 2 failures; with only 2 alive no progress is possible. That is consistency over availability.
tradeoffs: Each write costs a round trip to a majority, so cross-region clusters are slow.
Odd cluster sizes are cost-effective: 3 tolerates 1, 5 tolerates 2.
pitfalls: Running consensus clusters across high-latency links without testing.
Treating consensus as a general-purpose high-throughput database.
interview: Walk through a Raft leader election.
Why must a majority acknowledge before commit?

title: Probabilistic data structures
tagline: Answer 'have I seen this?' using a tiny fraction of the memory, with controlled error.
explain:
A Bloom filter is a bit array plus k hash functions. To add an item, set k bits; to query, check those k bits. If any bit is 0 the item is definitely absent; if all are 1 it is probably present (false positives possible, false negatives impossible).

False positive rate is about (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k, where n is items and m is bits. Roughly 10 bits per item with k=7 gives ~1%. You cannot delete (use a counting Bloom or cuckoo filter instead).

Uses: LSM databases check a Bloom filter before reading a file; web crawlers track seen URLs; caches avoid penetration (querying the DB for keys that do not exist); abuse and password-breach checks; CDN 'one-hit wonder' filtering.

Related structures for big data: HyperLogLog counts distinct items in ~12 KB with ~1% error; Count-Min Sketch estimates frequencies for top-k and heavy hitters; MinHash and SimHash estimate document similarity; t-digest estimates quantiles. Redis ships HLL, Bloom and top-k.

In interviews, say when exact answers are unnecessary and memory or throughput is the constraint.
tradeoffs: Memory drops by orders of magnitude at the price of a small error rate.
Filters are sized up front; overfilling raises the false-positive rate.
pitfalls: Using a Bloom filter where false positives are unacceptable without a confirm step.
Forgetting you cannot remove entries.
interview: How would you count unique visitors across 1B events with little memory?
Where does a Bloom filter help a database?

title: Queues, logs and streams
tagline: Decouple producers from consumers and absorb bursts.
explain:
A queue sits between a producer and consumers so each can run at its own speed.

Queue vs log: a message queue (SQS, RabbitMQ) deletes messages after consumption and is great for task distribution. A log (Kafka, Redpanda, Pulsar) retains messages; consumers track offsets, can replay history, and many independent consumer groups can read the same stream.

Kafka model: a topic has partitions; messages with the same key go to the same partition, so ordering is guaranteed per key. A consumer group splits partitions among its consumers, so parallelism is capped by the partition count. Adding a consumer triggers a rebalance.

Delivery semantics: at-most-once, at-least-once (default; duplicates possible), and effectively-once via idempotent consumers or transactions. Always make handlers idempotent.

Operations: monitor consumer lag (the key health metric), use dead-letter queues for poison messages, apply backpressure with bounded queues, and use the outbox pattern to publish events atomically with a database write.

Hot keys overload a single partition no matter how many consumers you add, so choose keys with care.
tradeoffs: Async processing smooths spikes but adds latency and operational surface.
More partitions allow more parallelism but make ordering per key the only ordering you get.
pitfalls: Non-idempotent consumers with at-least-once delivery.
Unbounded queues hiding overload until memory runs out.
Ignoring lag until users notice.
interview: Kafka vs SQS: how do you choose?
How do you guarantee ordering and still scale consumers?

title: Fan-out (feeds and timelines)
tagline: Do the work at write time or at read time. Mix both for celebrities.
explain:
Fan-out is delivering one event to many consumers, the heart of feeds, notifications and chat.

Fan-out on write (push): when a post is created, insert it into each follower's precomputed feed. Reads are one cheap lookup. Cost: a user with 10M followers triggers 10M writes, and most targets may never read.

Fan-out on read (pull): store posts once; when a user opens their feed, query the people they follow and merge. Writes are cheap; reads are expensive and slower.

Hybrid: push for normal users, pull for celebrities (above a follower threshold), merging celebrity posts into the precomputed feed at read time. Feeds live in a fast store (Redis lists or sorted sets) capped at N items, posts are hydrated from a post store by id, and ranking is a separate service.

Implementation details: write fan-out runs asynchronously through a queue and worker pool with batching; skip inactive users; handle unfollow and deletes lazily; keep per-user cursors for pagination; use idempotent inserts to survive retries.

The same trade-off appears in notification systems and group chat (small groups push, huge channels pull).
tradeoffs: Push optimizes read latency at write cost; pull optimizes write cost at read latency.
Hybrid adds complexity but is the usual production answer.
pitfalls: Ignoring the celebrity problem.
Fan-out in the request path instead of asynchronously.
No cap on stored feed length.
interview: Design a news feed. How do you handle a user with 50M followers?
What would you precompute and what would you compute at read time?

title: Dealing with contention
tagline: Many writers, one hot row: ticket sales, inventory, balances, flash sales.
explain:
Contention is many actors racing to change the same data. A read-modify-write sequence without protection loses updates.

Options, from simplest to most scalable:

- Atomic operations: UPDATE ... SET bal = bal - 30 WHERE bal >= 30, or Redis DECR. One statement, no race. Best when the invariant is simple.
- Pessimistic locking: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE holds a row lock until commit. Correct and simple; blocks other writers, risks deadlocks and long waits.
- Optimistic concurrency: read a version, write with WHERE version = X, retry on conflict. Great when conflicts are rare; wastes work when they are frequent.
- Serializable transactions: the database aborts conflicting transactions; retry.
- Distributed locks and leases: needed across systems; use fencing tokens so a paused client cannot write after losing the lock.
- Reservation with expiry (ticketing): hold a seat for 10 minutes with a TTL, then confirm on payment, otherwise release.
- Queue serialization: route all operations for one entity through a single partition or actor, so they run one at a time.
- Sharding the hot item (split a counter into N sub-counters and sum on read).

For flash sales: absorb the burst with a queue or virtual waiting room, decrement inventory atomically in a fast store, and reconcile with the database asynchronously.
tradeoffs: Locks are simple and safe but reduce throughput on hot rows.
Optimistic control scales reads and low-conflict writes but needs retries.
pitfalls: Read-modify-write in application code.
Distributed locks with no fencing or expiry.
Holding locks across network calls.
interview: How do you prevent double-booking the last seat?
Optimistic vs pessimistic locking: when each?

title: Proximity and geospatial search
tagline: Find nearby things without scanning everything.
explain:
Searching 'restaurants within 2 km' over millions of points needs a spatial index.

- Grid / geohash: divide the world into cells; a geohash encodes a cell as a string where shared prefixes mean nearby. Index points by cell id in a normal database; to search, look up the user's cell and its neighbors (boundary problem: nearby points can sit in different cells), then sort by exact distance.
- Quadtree: recursively split dense areas into four, so crowded cities have small cells and oceans are huge. Kept in memory or rebuilt periodically.
- S2 and H3 (Google, Uber): cell systems on a sphere with consistent neighbor rings; H3 uses hexagons for uniform distance.
- R-tree / PostGIS: database-native spatial indexes for moderate scale.

Workflow: coarse filter by cells, then precise filter and ranking (distance, rating, open now). For moving objects (drivers), keep locations in an in-memory store updated frequently, sharded by cell, with a TTL so stale positions drop out.

Sizing: choose a cell size roughly the search radius so a 3x3 neighborhood covers it. Too small means many cells per query; too big means scanning many irrelevant points.
tradeoffs: Fine grids scan fewer points but need more cells per query.
Quadtrees adapt to density but are harder to shard and update.
pitfalls: Ignoring cell boundaries and neighbors.
Computing Euclidean distance on lat/long near poles or across the dateline.
Writing every GPS ping to a durable store.
interview: Design 'find nearby drivers'.
Geohash vs quadtree: when each?

title: Scaling reads and writes
tagline: A ladder of fixes, cheapest first.
explain:
Scaling reads, in order:

1. Optimize queries and indexes.
2. Add caching (CDN, app cache, Redis).
3. Add read replicas (watch replication lag).
4. Precompute or denormalize hot views (materialized views, search index).
5. Shard.

Scaling writes, in order:

1. Reduce write cost: batch, avoid unnecessary indexes, async non-critical writes.
2. Buffer through a queue or log to absorb bursts and write in batches.
3. Vertical scale and faster storage.
4. Partition/shard by a key that spreads load.
5. Switch storage engine: LSM-based stores (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, RocksDB) for append-heavy workloads.
6. Pre-aggregate: count in memory or stream processors and write summaries (a counter is not a row per click).
7. Handle hot keys: split into sub-keys, sample, or isolate.

Throughput numbers to remember: a single relational primary handles thousands of writes/s; heavy ingest (100k+/s) pushes you to partitioned logs and LSM stores.

Always measure the actual bottleneck (CPU, I/O, locks, network, connection count) before picking a fix.
tradeoffs: Each rung adds consistency or operational complexity.
Read scaling is easier than write scaling because reads can be copied.
pitfalls: Sharding when a missing index was the problem.
Adding replicas to fix a write bottleneck.
interview: Your database is at 90% CPU from reads. Walk through what you do.
How would you ingest 500k events/s?

title: Load balancing
tagline: Spread work evenly and keep traffic away from sick servers.
explain:
A load balancer distributes requests across servers and removes unhealthy ones.

L4 balancers forward TCP/UDP flows (fast, protocol agnostic). L7 balancers understand HTTP, can route by path or header, terminate TLS, retry, canary, and apply auth or rate limits.

Algorithms: round robin and weighted round robin (equal-cost requests); least connections or least outstanding requests (variable-cost requests); power of two choices (pick two at random, take the less loaded; near-optimal with tiny state); consistent hashing (affinity for caches or sessions).

Operations: active health checks and passive outlier ejection, connection draining on deploys, slow start for new instances, and keep-alive reuse. Make the balancer itself redundant (multiple nodes, anycast or DNS), and use global load balancing (GeoDNS, anycast) across regions.

Stateless services scale horizontally behind a balancer; keep session state in a shared store or signed tokens. Sticky sessions are a crutch that harms balance and failover.

LLM traffic differs: request cost varies by orders of magnitude, so round robin creates hot GPUs. Route by outstanding tokens or queue depth, and add prefix-affinity so conversations hit a replica with a warm KV cache.
tradeoffs: Stickiness gives cache locality but unbalances load and complicates failover.
L7 gives features at higher cost and a larger failure surface.
pitfalls: Health checks that only test the port, not the dependency chain.
A single load balancer as a single point of failure.
Retries behind the balancer amplifying overload.
interview: Why can round robin fail with variable request cost?
How do you deploy with zero downtime behind a load balancer?

title: Real-time updates
tagline: Pushing changes to clients: polling, SSE, WebSockets, and the connection fleet behind them.
explain:
Choose the lightest mechanism that meets the latency need.

- Short polling: client asks every N seconds. Simple, wasteful, delay up to N.
- Long polling: server holds the request until data arrives. Works everywhere; reconnect overhead.
- Server-Sent Events: one-way stream over HTTP with auto-reconnect. Ideal for notifications, dashboards and LLM token streams.
- WebSockets: bidirectional, low overhead, needed for chat, collaboration, games. Stateful, so deploys and scaling need care.
- Push notifications (APNs/FCM) for offline mobile users.

Scaling the connection tier: gateway servers hold the sockets (tens to hundreds of thousands each), a registry maps user to gateway, and a pub/sub system (Redis, Kafka, NATS) routes messages to the right gateway. Treat sockets as a fast path only: every message has a sequence number, and a reconnecting client asks for everything after its last seen number. Add heartbeats, jittered exponential reconnect backoff, and graceful draining on deploy.

For huge fan-out (live comments, sports scores) publish once to a channel and let edge nodes fan out; apply sampling or batching for the busiest rooms.
tradeoffs: WebSockets minimize latency but cost memory per connection and complicate load balancing.
SSE is simpler and proxy-friendly but one-way.
pitfalls: Treating the socket as the source of truth (messages lost on reconnect).
Reconnect stampedes after a gateway restart.
interview: Design live comments for a stream with 1M viewers.
How do you not lose messages when a client disconnects?

title: Handling large blobs
tagline: Videos, images and files: keep them out of your servers.
explain:
Never stream big files through your app servers. Pattern:

1. Client asks your API for an upload. The API creates a record and returns a presigned URL (or a multipart upload plan) for object storage (S3, GCS).
2. Client uploads directly to object storage in chunks, in parallel, resumable. Large files use multipart upload so a failure retries one part.
3. Storage emits an event on completion; a worker validates, scans for malware, creates thumbnails or transcodes (video into multiple bitrates/segments), and updates metadata.
4. Reads go through a CDN with signed URLs for access control. Adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH) serves small segments.

Metadata (owner, size, hash, status, permissions) lives in a database; the blob lives in object storage addressed by key. Content-addressable keys (hash of content) enable deduplication. Sync clients (Dropbox style) split files into chunks, hash each chunk, upload only changed chunks, and keep a manifest.

Operational: lifecycle rules move old objects to cold storage, set per-user quotas, and clean up abandoned multipart uploads.
tradeoffs: Direct-to-storage uploads scale and save bandwidth but need careful authorization and completion handling.
More video renditions improve playback but multiply storage and compute.
pitfalls: Proxying uploads through app servers.
Trusting client-reported file type or size.
No resumability for large files.
interview: Design file upload for 5 GB videos.
How would a sync client detect and upload only changed parts of a file?

title: Long-running tasks and multi-step workflows
tagline: Jobs that take minutes to days must survive crashes and be observable.
explain:
Do not hold an HTTP request open for slow work. Accept the job, return 202 with an id, process it asynchronously, and let the client poll, receive a webhook or stream progress.

Building blocks: a durable queue, workers with visibility timeouts and heartbeats (so crashed work returns to the queue), idempotent steps, retries with backoff, dead-letter queues, progress records and cancellation.

For multi-step processes (order, onboarding, an AI agent run) use a workflow engine with durable execution (Temporal, Step Functions, Inngest). It records every step result in an event history; after a crash it replays the history and continues, so you write straightforward code and get retries, timers, signals (human approval) and visibility. Alternatives: the saga pattern (each step has a compensating action) and the outbox pattern for reliable events.

Design rules: every external side effect has an idempotency key, steps are small and resumable, state is explicit and stored, timeouts exist at every level, and failed workflows are inspectable and replayable by humans.
tradeoffs: Workflow engines add infrastructure but remove huge amounts of retry and state code.
Sagas avoid distributed locks but expose intermediate states.
pitfalls: In-memory job state lost on deploy.
Non-idempotent steps retried by the engine.
No way to cancel or inspect a stuck run.
interview: Design a system that processes an uploaded video and notifies the user.
Why use durable execution for AI agents?

title: Sagas and distributed transactions
tagline: Consistency across services without a global lock.
explain:
A business operation (order: reserve stock, charge card, ship) spans several services with separate databases. Two-phase commit locks resources across all participants and blocks if the coordinator dies, so modern systems prefer sagas.

A saga is a sequence of local transactions, each paired with a compensating action that semantically undoes it (release stock, refund payment). If step k fails, run compensations for steps k-1 down to 1.

- Orchestration: a central coordinator (or workflow engine) calls each step and decides what to do on failure. Easier to reason about and monitor.
- Choreography: services publish events and react to each other. Looser coupling, harder to trace.

Requirements: steps and compensations are idempotent and retryable; use the outbox pattern so state change and event commit atomically; accept that other users can see intermediate states (an order that is 'paid' but not 'shipped'); design compensations for things that cannot be undone (an email already sent: send a correction).

Use a real transaction when everything lives in one database. Reach for 2PC only inside systems built for it (for example Spanner or XA in a controlled environment).
tradeoffs: Sagas scale and stay available but give eventual rather than atomic consistency.
Orchestration centralizes logic; choreography distributes it.
pitfalls: Compensations that can themselves fail without retry.
Treating a refund as always possible.
No visibility into saga state.
interview: Design checkout across inventory, payment and shipping services.
Saga vs 2PC: trade-offs?

title: Rate limiting
tagline: Protect shared resources from abusive or accidental overload.
explain:
A rate limiter rejects or delays requests beyond a quota, per user, API key, IP or tenant.

Algorithms:

- Token bucket: a bucket of capacity B refills at rate r; each request takes a token. Allows bursts up to B with long-run rate r. Most common.
- Leaky bucket: requests drain at a fixed rate; smooths output.
- Fixed window counter: simple, but allows 2x bursts at window edges.
- Sliding window log/counter: accurate, more memory or computation.

Distributed implementation: keep counters in Redis, updated atomically with a Lua script or INCR plus EXPIRE, keyed by (user, window). Central counting is accurate but adds a network hop and a dependency; local limiters with periodic sync are fast but can overshoot. Decide fail-open (availability) or fail-closed (protection) per route.

Responses: HTTP 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers. Limit on the right unit: requests, bytes, concurrency, and for LLM products tokens per minute plus spend caps.

Placement: at the edge or gateway for abuse, and inside services for fairness between tenants. Combine with load shedding when the whole system is overloaded.
tradeoffs: Strict global accuracy costs latency; approximate local limits are cheap.
Burst allowance helps real users but lets short spikes through.
pitfalls: Limiting by IP behind NAT or proxies.
No headers, so clients cannot back off properly.
Fail-open during a Redis outage letting an attack through.
interview: Design a distributed rate limiter for 10M users.
Token bucket vs sliding window: which and why?

title: Circuit breakers and fallbacks
tagline: Fail fast instead of piling up on a dependency that is already down.
explain:
When a dependency is slow or failing, callers that keep trying hold threads and connections until they all fail too (cascading failure). A circuit breaker watches the error and latency rate of calls to one dependency:

- Closed: normal. Failures are counted over a rolling window.
- Open: threshold exceeded. Calls fail immediately (or go to a fallback) for a cool-down period, giving the dependency room to recover.
- Half-open: after cool-down, allow a few trial calls. Success closes the breaker; failure reopens it.

Pair it with:

- Timeouts on every call (a breaker needs failures to count).
- Bulkheads: separate thread or connection pools per dependency so one cannot exhaust everything.
- Fallbacks: cached or stale data, a default, a smaller model, a queued retry later, or a clear error.
- Retries with exponential backoff and jitter, limited by a budget.
- Load shedding and priority, so critical traffic survives.

For LLM apps: keep a breaker per provider and model, and fail over to a secondary provider or a cheaper model when the primary opens.
tradeoffs: Aggressive thresholds protect dependencies but may trip on harmless blips.
Fallbacks keep the product usable but may return degraded results.
pitfalls: No timeouts, so failures never register.
One breaker for everything.
Retrying through an open breaker.
interview: Explain the states of a circuit breaker.
How would you design graceful degradation for a recommendations widget?

title: Retries, backoff and jitter
tagline: Retries fix transient errors and turn outages into disasters when done naively.
explain:
Retries are essential and dangerous. If each of 3 layers retries 3 times, one user action becomes 27 calls to the bottom service exactly when it is struggling.

Rules:

1. Retry only errors that can succeed later (timeouts, 429, 503, connection reset), never validation errors.
2. Make operations idempotent first (idempotency keys), or retries duplicate side effects.
3. Use exponential backoff: wait base x 2^attempt, capped.
4. Add jitter (randomize the wait). Without it clients synchronize into waves.
5. Cap total attempts and total time, and propagate a deadline.
6. Use a retry budget (for example retries are at most 10% of recent requests) so a global failure does not multiply traffic.
7. Retry at one layer, not every layer.
8. Respect Retry-After and server hints.
9. Combine with circuit breakers and load shedding so the server can reject quickly.

A server that degrades under overload (slower, then failing more) can enter a metastable state where retries keep it overloaded even after the original cause is fixed. Backoff plus jitter and load shedding are the cure.
tradeoffs: Longer backoff reduces load but increases user-visible latency.
Hedged requests lower tail latency at the cost of extra load.
pitfalls: Immediate retries.
Retrying non-idempotent writes.
Retries at every layer of the stack.
interview: How do retries cause a cascading failure and what prevents it?
What does full jitter mean?

title: LLM gateway
tagline: One front door for auth, limits, caching, routing and cost tracking across model providers.
explain:
An LLM gateway sits between your apps and model providers.

Responsibilities:

- Authentication and per-key policies; tenant and team budgets.
- Rate limiting by tokens per minute, requests and concurrent streams, with 429 and Retry-After.
- Caching: exact-match and provider prefix/prompt caching; semantic caching only with strict scoping.
- Routing: choose a model by task tier, cost and latency; fail over between providers using circuit breakers; keep prompts portable.
- Streaming passthrough with correct backpressure and disconnect handling (stop paying when the client leaves).
- Observability: trace every call with model, tokens, latency, cost and prompt version; redact PII.
- Safety hooks: input and output guardrails, policy checks.
- Cost accounting: reserve estimated tokens before the call, reconcile real usage after, write to a ledger.

Architecture: a stateless data plane that scales horizontally with hot-path state in Redis (counters, breaker state), and a control plane (Postgres) for keys, policies and routes pushed to data-plane nodes. Budget enforcement can be exact (central counter) or approximate (local counters with sync) depending on tolerance.

Build versus buy: start with an open-source gateway (LiteLLM and similar) and customize once requirements are clear.
tradeoffs: A central gateway simplifies governance but is a critical path that must be highly available.
Aggressive caching saves money but risks serving wrong or cross-tenant answers.
pitfalls: Prompt formats that do not port across providers during failover.
Logging full prompts with sensitive data.
Counting requests but not tokens.
interview: Design an LLM gateway for 50 teams with budgets and failover.
How do you enforce a spending cap without adding much latency?
